brief.topic: Georgia Tech CS 6603 — AI, Ethics, and Society
brief.outcome: A learner can explain the full course sequence, evaluate AI/ML systems in social and legal context, reason about data and statistical validity, identify bias, compare fairness definitions, audit predictive applications, choose mitigation strategies, and defend a responsible deployment or non-deployment decision.
brief.audience: Georgia Tech OMSCS learner or practitioner studying AI ethics and algorithmic fairness
brief.prerequisites: Prior programming experience and working knowledge of Python and Jupyter notebooks; the official course page lists no significant additional prerequisites.
brief.direction: Prompt-to-explanation, distinction, application, cloze, and type-in recall across the official 22-lesson sequence.

sources.notes: Official Georgia Tech lesson index. The deck follows its 22-lesson order from Introduction through AI, Society, and Ethics Wrap-Up.

sources.title: ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct
sources.notes: Professional responsibilities for computing practitioners, including avoiding harm, fairness, privacy, and public good.

sources.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
sources.notes: Risk-management framework organized around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.

sources.title: NIST SP 1270 — Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence
sources.notes: NIST discussion of systemic, computational/statistical, and human-cognitive sources of bias across the AI lifecycle.

sources.title: OECD AI Principles
sources.notes: International principles emphasizing inclusive growth, human-centered values, transparency, robustness, security, and accountability.

sources.title: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
sources.notes: Global policy framework covering proportionality, do no harm, fairness, privacy, human oversight, transparency, and sustainability.

sources.title: FTC — Big Data: A Tool for Inclusion or Exclusion?
sources.notes: Archived official FTC report on data practices, discrimination risk, accuracy, transparency, and the use of big data in decisions; the live FTC URL has moved over time.

sources.title: European Union General Data Protection Regulation
sources.notes: Primary legal text for principles including purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, transparency, and data-subject rights.

sources.title: White House — Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights
sources.notes: Policy blueprint organized around safe and effective systems, algorithmic discrimination protections, data privacy, notice/explanation, and human alternatives.

sources.title: American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values
sources.notes: Guidance on interpreting p-values, uncertainty, practical importance, and the limits of binary significance decisions.

sources.title: Hernán and Robins — Causal Inference: What If
sources.notes: Open causal-inference text covering counterfactuals, confounding, intervention, identification, and observational studies.

sources.title: Caliskan, Bryson, and Narayanan — Semantics derived automatically from language corpora contain human-like biases
sources.notes: Introduces the Word Embedding Association Test and evidence that corpus-derived representations encode social associations.

sources.title: Bolukbasi et al. — Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker?
sources.notes: Classic work on detecting and reducing gender associations in word embeddings, including limitations of geometric debiasing.

sources.title: NIST Face Recognition Vendor Test — Demographic Effects
sources.notes: NIST evaluation reporting demographic variation in face-recognition error rates and the role of algorithms, data, and application context.

sources.title: U.S. EEOC — Employment Tests and Selection Procedures
sources.notes: Legal and statistical guidance for evaluating selection procedures, adverse impact, validation, and job-relatedness.

sources.title: ProPublica — Machine Bias
sources.notes: Case study of competing claims about racial disparities in the COMPAS recidivism-risk system and the importance of metric choice.

sources.title: Kleinberg, Mullainathan, and Raghavan — Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores
sources.notes: Shows conditions under which calibration and error-rate balance cannot all hold simultaneously when base rates differ.

sources.title: Fairlearn documentation
sources.notes: Open-source toolkit and documentation for assessing and mitigating fairness concerns in machine-learning systems.

sources.title: IBM AI Fairness 360 documentation
sources.notes: Toolkit documentation for fairness metrics, explainers, and preprocessing, in-processing, and post-processing algorithms.

sources.title: Mitchell et al. — Model Cards for Model Reporting
sources.notes: Proposes structured documentation of intended use, performance across conditions, limitations, and ethical considerations.

sources.title: Gebru et al. — Datasheets for Datasets
sources.notes: Proposes documentation of dataset motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and limitations.

sources.title: Google — Machine Learning Crash Course
sources.notes: Reference for supervised learning, train/validation/test splits, overfitting, classification, thresholds, and evaluation metrics.

claims.text: Why can an AI decision system create social harm even when its model is technically accurate? — Accuracy is only one property. A system can optimize the wrong target, use unfair or nonrepresentative data, distribute errors unevenly, remove due process, or scale a harmful decision.

claims.text: The course moves from {{c1::data, individuals, and society}} through big-data statistics and AI/ML techniques to bias mitigation and future opportunities. What does this progression emphasize? — Responsible AI reasoning should connect social context, data quality, statistical validity, technical models, evaluation, and intervention rather than treating them as separate topics.

claims.text: What makes a claim about an AI system an argument rather than merely an opinion? — It states a position, identifies relevant evidence and assumptions, addresses plausible counterarguments, and explains trade-offs and implications.

An acceptable prototype can produce unacceptable outcomes in a different institution or context.

claims.text: What is the difference between bias as a statistical property and bias as a social concern? — Statistical bias is systematic error relative to a target or estimator; social bias concerns unequal, unjust, or harmful treatment, representation, or outcomes. They can overlap but are not interchangeable.
claims.evidenceExcerpt: Statistical bias is systematic error relative to a target or estimator; social bias concerns unequal, unjust, or harmful treatment, representation, or outcomes. They can overlap but are not interchangeable.

claims.text: Why can an ethical dilemma not be resolved by simply naming a principle? — Principles can conflict: privacy may limit fairness auditing, transparency may expose security risks, and equal error rates may conflict with calibration. cards.front: What is the central problem CS 6603 asks learners to analyze?
cards.back: How data, AI, and machine-learning systems affect individuals and society, including fairness, bias, ethics, legality, collection, deployment, and public use.
cards.extra: Treat the course as a sociotechnical analysis: the model is only one component of a larger system.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can an AI decision system create social harm even when its model is technically accurate?
cards.back: Accuracy is only one property. A system can optimize the wrong target, use unfair or nonrepresentative data, distribute errors unevenly, remove due process, or scale a harmful decision.
cards.extra: Ask who defines success, who bears errors, and what happens after the prediction enters a real institution.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: The course moves from {{c1::data, individuals, and society}} through big-data statistics and AI/ML techniques to bias mitigation and future opportunities. What does this progression emphasize?
cards.back: Responsible AI reasoning should connect social context, data quality, statistical validity, technical models, evaluation, and intervention rather than treating them as separate topics.
cards.extra: This is the official four-module arc of the course.
cards.typeRationale: The deletion targets a single course term inside a stable context.

cards.front: What makes a claim about an AI system an argument rather than merely an opinion?
cards.back: It states a position, identifies relevant evidence and assumptions, addresses plausible counterarguments, and explains trade-offs and implications.
cards.extra: CS 6603 explicitly allows differing viewpoints while requiring thoughtful, well-supported reasoning.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What five-part system should you map before judging an AI application?
cards.back: The data-generating process, the model or algorithm, the decision or action, the people and institutions affected, and the deployment and feedback environment.
cards.extra: This map prevents a narrow focus on model internals from hiding organizational or social causes of harm.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the difference between allocative harm and representational harm?
cards.back: Allocative harm withholds or misallocates an opportunity or resource; representational harm devalues, stereotypes, erases, or mischaracterizes people or groups.
cards.extra: A system can create both: a hiring score can affect access to jobs and encode degrading assumptions about applicants.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What responsibility does the ACM Code place on computing professionals when a system may cause harm?
cards.back: Professionals should contribute to the public good, avoid harm, be fair, respect privacy, evaluate risks, and communicate relevant limitations rather than hiding behind the system's automation.
cards.extra: Professional responsibility continues through design, deployment, monitoring, and retirement.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why does CS 6603 treat deployment as part of the ethical analysis rather than the final technical step?
cards.back: Real-world use changes incentives, populations, error costs, power relationships, and feedback. An acceptable prototype can produce unacceptable outcomes in a different institution or context.
cards.extra: Use a lifecycle view: define, collect, build, validate, deploy, monitor, respond, and retire.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What are the four primary modules of CS 6603?
cards.back: 1) Data, Individuals, and Society; 2) The BS of Big Data and Stats 101; 3) AI/ML Techniques; and 4) Bias Mitigation Applications, also framed as applications and future opportunities.
cards.extra: The lesson order is preserved in the official Georgia Tech course-video index.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why is the data-to-model-to-decision chain useful for ethical analysis?
cards.back: It separates where a problem may enter: data collection can encode exclusion, modeling can amplify patterns, decision rules can impose unequal costs, and deployment can create feedback.
cards.extra: Trace the chain in both directions because decisions can later change the data that are collected.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the difference between bias as a statistical property and bias as a social concern?
cards.back: Statistical bias is systematic error relative to a target or estimator; social bias concerns unequal, unjust, or harmful treatment, representation, or outcomes. They can overlap but are not interchangeable.
cards.extra: A statistically unbiased estimator can still optimize an ethically unacceptable target.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is a normative question in AI ethics?
cards.back: A question about what should be valued, permitted, required, or prohibited, such as whether a use is justifiable or which error trade-off is acceptable.
cards.extra: Empirical evidence can inform a normative decision, but it does not by itself settle the value judgment.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Which stakeholders belong in an AI impact map?
cards.back: Data subjects, direct users, people evaluated or affected, operators and decision makers, developers, deployers, institutions, regulators, auditors, and communities indirectly affected.
cards.extra: Include people who lack the power to opt out or contest an outcome.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What kinds of risk should be considered together in a responsible-AI review?
cards.back: Validity and reliability, fairness and discrimination, privacy and security, safety, transparency and contestability, legal compliance, labor and environmental effects, and institutional accountability.
cards.extra: NIST AI RMF provides a useful risk-management structure, but no framework replaces contextual judgment.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why is there rarely one universal fairness answer for an AI system?
cards.back: Fairness depends on the decision, stakeholders, protected interests, base rates, error costs, legal setting, and whether the goal is equal opportunity, equal outcomes, calibrated risk, or another conception.
cards.extra: Make the fairness construct explicit before selecting a metric.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What study habit does the course overview encourage when reading an AI case?
cards.back: Separate facts from value judgments, identify assumptions and affected parties, test technical claims, compare alternative interventions, and state trade-offs and uncertainty.
cards.extra: This habit turns a case summary into a defensible critique.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How do ethics and law differ?
cards.back: Law consists of enforceable rules made by authorized institutions; ethics concerns principles and reasons about what ought to be done. Law can express ethical values but is not identical to moral justification.
cards.extra: A legal permission is not automatically an ethical endorsement, and an ethical concern may precede legislation.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does it mean to say that legal compliance is a floor rather than a ceiling?
cards.back: Compliance establishes minimum obligations; responsible practice may require additional care for dignity, fairness, privacy, safety, or public trust beyond what a rule explicitly demands.
cards.extra: Use this distinction without claiming that ethics permits ignoring law.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is consequentialist reasoning?
cards.back: It evaluates an action or policy primarily by its expected consequences, such as benefits, harms, distribution of outcomes, and affected interests.
cards.extra: A consequentialist analysis still must specify whose consequences count and how uncertainty is handled.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is deontological reasoning?
cards.back: It evaluates duties, rules, rights, or constraints that should be respected even when violating them might produce attractive aggregate results.
cards.extra: Consent, non-discrimination, privacy, and due process can function as constraints rather than merely inputs to a utility calculation.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How can virtue ethics contribute to an AI design decision?
cards.back: It asks what a good professional or institution would do and which character traits—such as honesty, humility, courage, care, and justice—the practice should cultivate.
cards.extra: Virtue reasoning is useful for accountability and professional conduct but does not eliminate the need to examine concrete outcomes.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is procedural justice in an automated decision process?
cards.back: It concerns the fairness of the process: notice, understandable reasons, consistent treatment, an opportunity to be heard, review by an appropriate decision maker, and a meaningful route to correction or appeal.
cards.extra: A procedurally fair process can still produce substantively unfair results, so evaluate both.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can an ethical dilemma not be resolved by simply naming a principle?
cards.back: Principles can conflict: privacy may limit fairness auditing, transparency may expose security risks, and equal error rates may conflict with calibration. The analyst must explain scope, priorities, trade-offs, and affected parties.
cards.extra: A reasoned decision is stronger than a slogan such as “be fair.”
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the relationship between professional codes and organizational policy?
cards.back: A professional code provides duties and values for practitioners; organizational policy operationalizes responsibilities in a particular setting. Neither removes the professional's duty to recognize and escalate harmful practices.
cards.extra: Document who has authority, what review exists, and how dissent or whistleblowing is handled.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What question should a legal analysis ask before applying a regulation to an AI system?
cards.back: What activity, jurisdiction, protected interest, actor, data, decision, and legal test the rule actually covers, including definitions, exceptions, enforcement, and available remedies.
cards.extra: Avoid treating a broad policy summary as a legal conclusion.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why is data collection a normative act rather than a neutral prelude to modeling?
cards.back: Collectors choose what to observe, whom to include, how to define variables, what purposes are acceptable, and which behaviors become legible to an institution.
cards.extra: The absence of a group from a dataset can be a consequence of power, access, or surveillance rather than evidence that the group does not matter.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the difference between notice and meaningful consent?
cards.back: Notice communicates a practice; meaningful consent involves understandable information, voluntariness, a real choice, and an appropriate ability to refuse or withdraw when consent is the basis for collection.
cards.extra: A long policy accepted under dependency or coercion may provide notice without meaningful choice.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is purpose limitation?
cards.back: Data should be collected for specified, explicit, legitimate purposes and not later reused in incompatible ways without justification or a new lawful basis.
cards.extra: Purpose limitation is a governance constraint against function creep.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: The principle of {{c1::data minimization}} asks an organization to collect only data that are adequate, relevant, and necessary for a stated purpose. Why does this matter for AI?
cards.back: Less unnecessary data reduces exposure, secondary-use risk, surveillance, storage burden, and the number of irrelevant or sensitive proxies a model can learn.
cards.extra: More data is not automatically more legitimate or more accurate.
cards.typeRationale: The deletion targets a single course term inside a stable context.

cards.front: What is surveillance asymmetry?
cards.back: An institution can observe and classify people who cannot meaningfully observe, understand, or challenge the institution's data practices and inferences.
cards.extra: Asymmetry raises power, privacy, consent, and due-process concerns even when a person has technically visible behavior.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why are proxy variables ethically important?
cards.back: A variable can encode or reconstruct a protected or sensitive attribute even when that attribute is omitted, allowing a system to reproduce unequal treatment while appearing neutral.
cards.extra: Examples include location, names, education histories, language, and network structure; context determines the risk.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How can missing data create unfairness?
cards.back: Missingness may be concentrated in certain groups or generated by unequal access, nonresponse, measurement failure, or institutional decisions. Imputation can hide that process and introduce new error.
cards.extra: Analyze the mechanism of missingness, not just the percentage missing.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why does the label-generation process matter?
cards.back: Labels often reflect human judgment, institutional policy, historical inequality, or selective observation rather than an objective ground truth. A model can faithfully learn a harmful label.
cards.extra: Ask who labeled, under what incentives, with what information, and whose outcomes were never observed.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How can seemingly anonymous data be re-identifiable?
cards.back: Combining quasi-identifiers such as dates, locations, demographics, or behavioral traces with outside data can narrow records to people; rare combinations are especially revealing.
cards.extra: Anonymization claims should be tested against realistic auxiliary data and adversaries.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What should a data-governance record preserve about a dataset?
cards.back: Provenance, purpose, collection method, population and exclusions, consent or legal basis, transformations, labels, access controls, retention, known limitations, and accountable owners.
cards.extra: Datasheets and similar documentation make hidden assumptions inspectable; they do not by themselves guarantee ethical use.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is pre-existing bias?
cards.back: Bias already present in social institutions, historical records, categories, incentives, or unequal opportunities before a system is designed.
cards.extra: A model may reproduce pre-existing bias even when the engineering process is internally consistent.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is technical bias?
cards.back: Bias introduced or amplified by choices in measurement, sampling, labeling, feature construction, modeling, evaluation, thresholds, or implementation.
cards.extra: Technical bias is not necessarily caused by a malicious designer; it can arise from a mismatch between abstraction and use.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is emergent bias?
cards.back: Bias that appears when a system is used in a context, population, task, or interaction different from the conditions assumed during design and testing.
cards.extra: Distribution shift and institutional feedback are common sources of emergent bias.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How does measurement bias differ from representation bias?
cards.back: Measurement bias makes a variable an inaccurate or differently constructed measure of the intended concept; representation bias makes the data population or coverage unrepresentative of the relevant population.
cards.extra: A well-sampled dataset can still measure the wrong construct, and a valid measure can still be absent for a group.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is aggregation bias?
cards.back: Using one model, feature representation, or decision rule across groups whose relationships between inputs and outcomes differ in ways the shared representation cannot capture.
cards.extra: A single average model can perform acceptably overall while failing systematically for subgroups.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How can a benchmark create bias?
cards.back: Its task definition, labels, sampling, categories, language, image quality, or evaluation metric can privilege some users and make performance appear better than it is in deployment.
cards.extra: Benchmark performance is evidence under specified conditions, not a universal property of a system.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is a feedback loop in an algorithmic decision system?
cards.back: A decision changes behavior, opportunities, or observations, and those changed data are later used to retrain or justify the same decision, reinforcing an initial pattern.
cards.extra: Predictive policing is a canonical example: policing creates records that then guide more policing.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why is bias not identical to discrimination?
cards.back: Bias describes systematic skew or error; discrimination concerns unjust differential treatment or impact in a social and legal context. A biased measurement may not map directly to a prohibited decision, and discrimination can occur without an obvious statistical bias.
cards.extra: Keep statistical diagnosis and normative/legal judgment distinct but connected.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why should fairness analysis consider intersectionality?
cards.back: People occupy overlapping social positions, and a model can appear fair for each broad group while failing badly for an intersection such as race-by-gender or disability-by-age.
cards.extra: Always inspect meaningful subgroup slices when data and privacy constraints permit.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What makes a fairness claim context-dependent?
cards.back: The relevant harm, decision, baseline, protected interest, affected group, time horizon, and remedy determine which evidence and fairness criterion are appropriate.
cards.extra: Start with the decision and harm, then choose measurements; do not start with a favorite metric.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What skepticism is captured by the phrase “The BS of Big Data”?
cards.back: Large datasets and sophisticated tools can create an illusion of objectivity while hiding biased collection, invalid proxies, confounding, overfitting, bad labels, and unjustified conclusions.
cards.extra: Scale can magnify a flawed measurement rather than correct it.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What do the common dimensions of big data describe?
cards.back: Volume is amount, velocity is rate of generation or use, variety is heterogeneity of formats and sources, and veracity concerns reliability, provenance, and uncertainty.
cards.extra: These dimensions describe engineering conditions; none guarantees fairness or truth.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why does more data not automatically eliminate bias?
cards.back: More observations can reproduce the same selection process, labels, measurement errors, historical inequities, or feedback loops at greater scale.
cards.extra: Ask whether additional data improve coverage and construct validity, not only sample size.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is overfitting?
cards.back: A model learns idiosyncrasies or noise in the training data rather than a pattern that generalizes to new cases.
cards.extra: Overfit models can look impressive on training data and fail silently in deployment.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why is data leakage dangerous?
cards.back: Information unavailable at prediction time, or derived from the outcome or future, enters features or preprocessing, producing unrealistically strong evaluation results.
cards.extra: Leakage is a validity failure before it is a fairness failure, but it can also create group-specific harm in deployment.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the difference between correlation and causation?
cards.back: Correlation is statistical association; causation concerns how an intervention or change in one variable would alter an outcome under a specified causal model.
cards.extra: An accurate correlation may still be useless or harmful as a basis for intervention.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why should data analysis distinguish exploratory from confirmatory work?
cards.back: Exploration generates hypotheses and can search many patterns; confirmation tests pre-specified claims with appropriate uncertainty accounting. Treating exploration as confirmation inflates confidence.
cards.extra: Record analysis choices and separate discovery from validation.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does a reproducible data pipeline make visible?
cards.back: Inputs, versions, transformations, exclusions, random seeds, code, model settings, evaluation slices, and outputs needed to repeat or audit an analysis.
cards.extra: Reproducibility supports accountability but cannot make an invalid or unethical design valid.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: In a supervised-learning table, what are features, labels, and rows?
cards.back: Features are input variables, the label is the target outcome or class to predict, and each row represents an example or unit of analysis under the dataset's definition.
cards.extra: The row definition determines whether observations are independent and what population the model describes.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why should a data analyst distinguish categorical, ordinal, count, continuous, and binary variables?
cards.back: Their meanings, valid operations, encodings, missing-value behavior, and statistical assumptions differ; treating categories as arbitrary numbers can invent misleading distances.
cards.extra: Type is about measurement meaning, not only the storage format.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the purpose of a train/validation/test split?
cards.back: Training fits the model, validation supports model or hyperparameter choices, and the held-out test estimates performance on unseen data after choices are fixed.
cards.extra: Do not repeatedly tune against the test set and then call it independent evidence.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can a fixed random seed improve an analysis without making it unbiased?
cards.back: It makes a stochastic split or procedure reproducible so others can inspect and compare it; it does not correct nonrepresentative sampling or guarantee a good split.
cards.extra: Reproducibility and validity are separate properties.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What risks arise when missing values are silently dropped?
cards.back: Dropping rows can change the target population and disproportionately remove groups; dropping columns can discard signal or create a new proxy for missingness.
cards.extra: Report how missingness varies by relevant subgroup and what mechanism may have generated it.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can one-hot encoding be safer than numeric labels for unordered categories?
cards.back: It represents category membership without implying that category 3 is more or less than category 1 or that their difference has a meaningful magnitude.
cards.extra: The best encoding still depends on the model and the construct.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does standardization do, and what does it not do?
cards.back: It rescales a numeric variable, often by subtracting a mean and dividing by a standard deviation; it does not make the variable normally distributed, causally meaningful, or fair.
cards.extra: Fit transformations on training data when evaluating generalization.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why should exploratory plots be paired with an explicit data dictionary?
cards.back: A plot can reveal patterns, but without definitions, units, collection rules, and valid ranges the analyst may misread a code, category, or aggregation.
cards.extra: Visualization is a reasoning aid, not a substitute for provenance.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the difference between descriptive and inferential statistics?
cards.back: Descriptive statistics summarize observed data; inferential statistics use a sampling or probabilistic model to reason about a wider population or uncertainty beyond the observed sample.
cards.extra: Inference inherits the assumptions and sampling process that produced the data.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: When is the median more informative than the mean?
cards.back: When the distribution is skewed or contains influential outliers, because the median is the middle order statistic and is less sensitive to extreme values.
cards.extra: Neither statistic is automatically the right summary; connect it to the decision and distribution.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What do variance and standard deviation measure?
cards.back: They summarize dispersion around the mean; variance uses squared deviations and standard deviation is its square root in the original units.
cards.extra: A large spread can reflect real heterogeneity, measurement noise, or a mixture of populations.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does the interquartile range measure?
cards.back: The distance between the 75th and 25th percentiles, covering the middle half of observations and providing a robust spread summary.
cards.extra: IQR-based summaries are useful when tails or outliers make variance unstable.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does a right-skewed distribution imply about mean and median?
cards.back: A long right tail often pulls the mean above the median, but the exact relationship depends on the distribution and should be checked rather than assumed.
cards.extra: Report shape and tail behavior when a single center would conceal important cases.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why should outliers be investigated before deletion?
cards.back: They may be errors, rare but valid cases, a subgroup, fraud, or a consequence of a measurement process. Deleting them can change the question and disproportionately remove people.
cards.extra: Use domain rules, provenance, robust methods, and sensitivity analysis.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does a correlation coefficient summarize?
cards.back: The direction and strength of a particular form of association, commonly linear association for Pearson correlation, under the chosen variables and population.
cards.extra: Correlation is sensitive to outliers and does not establish causation.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the ecological fallacy?
cards.back: Inferring individual-level relationships from aggregate-level data, or assuming that a pattern across groups must hold for members within each group.
cards.extra: Disaggregate when the decision concerns individuals and interpret group summaries at their proper level.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can normalization or a rate denominator change the story?
cards.back: Rates compare quantities relative to a population at risk; choosing a denominator, time window, or aggregation level changes what the statistic means and which groups appear large or small.
cards.extra: Always name the numerator, denominator, unit, and time period.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is Simpson's paradox?
cards.back: A relationship seen in several groups can reverse or disappear after the groups are combined because group composition or a confounding variable changes the aggregate weighting.
cards.extra: Inspect stratified results before trusting a single overall average.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the ethical risk of a dashboard that reports only an overall average?
cards.back: It can conceal subgroup harms, unequal coverage, uncertainty, tail outcomes, missingness, and changes in population composition behind a seemingly precise summary.
cards.extra: Pair aggregate metrics with disaggregated, distributional, and uncertainty views.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the target population?
cards.back: The full population or set of units to which the analysis intends to generalize a claim or decision.
cards.extra: Define it before looking at the sample; otherwise generalization can silently shrink to whoever was easiest to observe.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the accessible population?
cards.back: The portion of the target population that the collection process can actually reach under its channels, eligibility rules, time window, and resources.
cards.extra: A large sample from an inaccessible subset can still be biased for the target population.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is coverage bias?
cards.back: Systematic undercoverage or exclusion caused by the sampling frame failing to include parts of the target population.
cards.extra: Digital traces often underrepresent people with limited access, privacy protections, language support, or trust in the system.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How does self-selection bias arise?
cards.back: Participation depends on a person's willingness, ability, incentives, or experience, so respondents differ systematically from nonrespondents or nonusers.
cards.extra: Voluntary feedback can overrepresent both highly satisfied and highly dissatisfied users.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is nonresponse bias?
cards.back: The observed respondents differ from sampled units who do not respond in ways related to variables of interest or the outcome.
cards.extra: A high response rate does not prove absence of nonresponse bias, and a low rate does not quantify its direction by itself.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is survivorship bias?
cards.back: Drawing conclusions from units that remain observable or successful while ignoring units that failed, exited, were excluded, or were never recorded.
cards.extra: Study the denominator and the missing cases, not only the visible winners.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is measurement or response bias in a survey?
cards.back: Answers or measurements systematically differ from the intended construct because of wording, social desirability, recall, interviewer effects, instrumentation, or incentives.
cards.extra: A response can be accurately recorded and still be a biased measure of the underlying concept.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: When can weighting help correct a sample?
cards.back: When selection probabilities or population benchmarks are known well enough to reweight observations toward the target population under defensible assumptions.
cards.extra: Weighting can increase variance and cannot repair an unmeasured group or a fundamentally invalid measurement.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is external validity?
cards.back: The credibility of applying a finding beyond the observed sample, setting, treatment, time, or measurement conditions.
cards.extra: External validity requires reasoning about transport, not merely a large n.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What should a sampling-bias audit document?
cards.back: The target and accessible populations, frame, recruitment, response and exclusion patterns, time window, subgroup coverage, missingness, weighting, and plausible directions of bias.
cards.extra: Make the path from population to dataset explicit before interpreting model performance.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does correlation establish?
cards.back: It describes an association in the observed data under a chosen statistical summary; it does not by itself identify the effect of changing one variable.
cards.extra: State the population, time order, and measurement before interpreting an association.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is a confounder?
cards.back: A variable that influences both the exposure or treatment and the outcome, creating or distorting their observed association when not appropriately controlled.
cards.extra: Control requires a causal argument; adding every available variable is not automatically valid.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is reverse causation?
cards.back: The apparent cause is partly or wholly an effect of the outcome, or the outcome changes the exposure over time.
cards.extra: Use temporal ordering and a causal model instead of assuming the direction implied by the data table.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can conditioning on a collider create bias?
cards.back: A collider is influenced by two variables; conditioning on it can make otherwise unrelated causes statistically associated by selecting a nonrepresentative path.
cards.extra: This is why “control for everything” is not a sound causal strategy.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the role of randomization in a controlled experiment?
cards.back: Random assignment makes treatment independent of measured and unmeasured pre-treatment factors in expectation, supporting a causal comparison under compliance and other assumptions.
cards.extra: Randomization does not automatically solve attrition, noncompliance, interference, or unethical treatment assignment.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does a causal DAG provide?
cards.back: A diagram of assumed causal relationships that helps identify confounders, mediators, colliders, adjustment sets, and paths that should or should not be conditioned on.
cards.extra: A DAG is an explicit model of assumptions, not proof that the arrows are true.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is a counterfactual outcome?
cards.back: The outcome that the same unit would have experienced under an alternative treatment or exposure, even though only one treatment is observed for that unit.
cards.extra: Causal effects compare potential outcomes under interventions, not merely similar-looking groups.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is Simpson's paradox in a causal setting?
cards.back: An aggregate association can reverse after stratifying by a third variable because group composition, treatment assignment, or causal structure differs across strata.
cards.extra: Always ask whether the aggregation mixes populations with different causal pathways.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why is a predictive model not automatically a causal model?
cards.back: Prediction can use any stable association that improves forecasts, while causal intervention requires assumptions about how variables change and what would happen under a policy.
cards.extra: A feature may be predictive but unsafe to manipulate or use for allocation.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What question should precede using an association to justify a policy?
cards.back: What intervention is proposed, which mechanism is assumed, what alternatives and confounders exist, whose outcomes change, and what evidence could distinguish the causal explanation from competing explanations.
cards.extra: Policy is an intervention; prediction alone is not its justification.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is a point estimate?
cards.back: A single statistic computed from a sample that estimates a population quantity, such as a mean, proportion, regression coefficient, or error rate.
cards.extra: The point does not express sampling uncertainty by itself.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is a confidence interval intended to communicate?
cards.back: An interval produced by a procedure with a stated long-run coverage property under its assumptions, giving a range of estimates compatible with sampling variability.
cards.extra: A 95% interval is not literally a 95% probability statement about a fixed parameter in the frequentist interpretation.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is standard error?
cards.back: A measure of the sampling variability of an estimator under a model or resampling procedure.
cards.extra: Standard error is uncertainty about an estimate, not the spread of individual observations.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How does sample size usually affect a standard error?
cards.back: With comparable independent observations and a suitable estimator, more observations usually reduce sampling variability, often at a rate related to 1 over the square root of n.
cards.extra: More data do not fix systematic bias, dependence, or a poor target measure.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does a margin of error represent?
cards.back: A chosen uncertainty radius around an estimate under a specified confidence procedure and assumptions.
cards.extra: Name the confidence level, sampling design, estimator, and population when reporting it.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is a p-value?
cards.back: Under a specified null model and analysis procedure, the probability of data at least as extreme as the observed data; it is not the probability that the null is true.
cards.extra: The ASA cautions against treating a threshold crossing as a complete measure of evidence or importance.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is statistical power?
cards.back: The probability that a chosen test detects an effect of a specified size under a particular alternative, design, noise level, and decision threshold.
cards.extra: Low power makes a non-significant result weak evidence of no effect; high power does not make an effect important.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: When is bootstrapping useful?
cards.back: When resampling from observed data can approximate the sampling distribution of a statistic and the sample reasonably represents the process of interest.
cards.extra: Bootstrap intervals inherit the sample's selection and measurement problems.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why do multiple comparisons increase false-positive risk?
cards.back: Testing many hypotheses creates more opportunities for at least one extreme result by chance unless the analysis accounts for the search or controls an appropriate error rate.
cards.extra: Pre-registration, holdout validation, correction, and replication address different parts of the problem.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why distinguish statistical significance from practical significance?
cards.back: A tiny effect can be statistically detectable with a large sample, while a meaningful effect can be uncertain in a small sample. Decisions require magnitude, uncertainty, costs, and context.
cards.extra: Do not reduce a policy decision to p < 0.05.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the distributional hypothesis?
cards.back: Words occurring in similar contexts tend to have related meanings or uses, so context patterns can provide a basis for learning representations.
cards.extra: It is a useful linguistic hypothesis, not a claim that context fully determines meaning or social value.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why are dense word embeddings different from one-hot vectors?
cards.back: A one-hot vector marks one vocabulary item with a sparse coordinate; a dense embedding represents each item with a learned low-dimensional vector whose geometry can encode patterns of use.
cards.extra: Dense geometry is useful but can also carry and amplify corpus associations.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does a word-embedding vector represent?
cards.back: A learned numerical representation derived from a training objective and corpus context; its dimensions generally do not have simple human-interpretable meanings.
cards.extra: Interpret similarity behavior empirically rather than assigning a moral or semantic meaning to one coordinate.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does cosine similarity compare?
cards.back: The angle between two vectors, often used to compare their direction while reducing sensitivity to vector magnitude.
cards.extra: Similarity is relative to the training corpus, preprocessing, vocabulary, and model; it is not a universal semantic truth.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How can context-window choices affect an embedding?
cards.back: A narrow window may emphasize syntactic or local relations; a wider window may capture broader topical or associative relations. The choice changes what “similar” means.
cards.extra: Model architecture and training data jointly define the representation.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the intuition behind analogy arithmetic in embeddings?
cards.back: Some semantic or syntactic relations may appear as approximate vector directions, so subtracting one term and adding another can retrieve a nearby term.
cards.extra: Analogy success is a property of a trained geometry, not proof that a relation is universally valid.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why does corpus provenance matter for an embedding?
cards.back: The corpus reflects which people, genres, time periods, languages, and institutions are represented, along with its stereotypes, omissions, licenses, and preprocessing choices.
cards.extra: A model card should identify intended data and known limitations rather than calling an embedding generic.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How can polysemy challenge a single word vector?
cards.back: One vector may collapse multiple senses or social contexts of a word, making similarity reflect a mixture of meanings and potentially hiding subgroup-specific behavior.
cards.extra: Contextual representations can separate senses better but introduce their own training and evaluation risks.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why is an embedding not just a passive dictionary?
cards.back: It is an optimized representation shaped by an objective, corpus, sampling, and model architecture, and it can influence downstream classifications, rankings, and recommendations.
cards.extra: Representational choices become consequential when a downstream system treats them as evidence.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is a responsible first question before deploying a pretrained embedding?
cards.back: What task, users, languages, populations, and harms is it intended for, and what evidence shows that its behavior is valid and acceptable in that context?
cards.extra: Reuse is not neutral just because training happened elsewhere.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does bias in a word embedding mean?
cards.back: The representation encodes systematic associations or performance differences that reflect social stereotypes, corpus imbalance, measurement choices, or unequal language use.
cards.extra: The word “bias” needs a task, comparison, and harm context; not every statistical association is an injustice.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does the Word Embedding Association Test attempt to measure?
cards.back: A difference in association strength between target word sets and attribute word sets, using a test statistic and effect size based on vector similarity.
cards.extra: WEAT is a diagnostic for a representation under specified word lists; it is not a complete audit of a deployed NLP system.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is representational harm in a language model or embedding?
cards.back: A system stereotypes, demeans, erases, or mischaracterizes people or groups in the meanings, associations, or language it produces or ranks.
cards.extra: Representational harm can matter even when no immediate allocation decision is made.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How can corpus composition produce gender or racial associations?
cards.back: Historical text, occupational segregation, stereotypes, unequal authorship, media framing, and differing quantities or contexts of language can become statistical regularities the model learns.
cards.extra: The model may encode the world as observed rather than the world users want to reproduce.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the basic idea of geometric debiasing by projection?
cards.back: Identify a direction associated with a protected concept, then remove or reduce components of vectors along that direction while trying to preserve desired relations.
cards.extra: Projection can reduce one measured association without removing all stereotypes or ensuring fair downstream behavior.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can debiasing an embedding create a false sense of safety?
cards.back: Bias may be encoded in many directions, relational structures, vocabulary gaps, or downstream data; removing a selected axis can hide a diagnostic while preserving harmful behavior.
cards.extra: Evaluate the actual task and multiple subgroups after any mitigation.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why does intersectional evaluation matter for word embeddings?
cards.back: Associations involving combined identities may be invisible in separate gender or race tests, while downstream language can be especially harmful for less represented intersections.
cards.extra: Use meaningful target and attribute sets and report uncertainty and coverage.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic embedding evaluation?
cards.back: Intrinsic evaluation tests representation properties such as similarity or analogy; extrinsic evaluation measures performance and harms when the representation is used in a downstream task.
cards.extra: A better intrinsic score does not necessarily imply a fairer application.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can fairness and utility appear to trade off in embedding mitigation?
cards.back: Removing associations may reduce information useful for a target task, while preserving associations may retain stereotypes. The trade-off depends on what is considered utility and whose costs are counted.
cards.extra: Make the task and protected interest explicit instead of treating utility as neutral.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What should an NLP deployment document about social bias?
cards.back: Training sources, languages and populations, evaluation sets, known associations, subgroup performance, intended and excluded uses, mitigation steps, residual risk, and a monitoring and redress plan.
cards.extra: Documentation should be evidence for a decision, not a substitute for one.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What are the main stages of a face-recognition pipeline?
cards.back: Capture, face detection, alignment or normalization, feature extraction or representation, comparison or classification, thresholding, and a decision or human review action.
cards.extra: A fairness issue can enter at any stage, not only in the final classifier.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the difference between face verification and face identification?
cards.back: Verification is a one-to-one question about whether a face matches a claimed identity; identification is a one-to-many search for a likely identity in a gallery.
cards.extra: One-to-many search usually creates different base rates, error exposure, and due-process concerns.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is a false positive in face recognition?
cards.back: The system reports a match or identity when the person is not the claimed or returned identity.
cards.extra: In a surveillance or enforcement context, a false positive can trigger investigation or loss of liberty rather than merely a failed login.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is a false negative in face recognition?
cards.back: The system fails to match a person who should have been matched or fails to recognize a claimed identity.
cards.extra: The social cost depends on context: access denial, missed assistance, or an escape from an unjust system are different harms.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How does threshold selection affect face-recognition errors?
cards.back: A stricter threshold generally reduces some false matches while increasing missed matches; a looser threshold does the opposite, with effects that can differ by group and context.
cards.extra: The threshold is a policy choice tied to error costs, not a purely technical setting.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does an ROC curve show in a recognition system?
cards.back: The trade-off between true-positive and false-positive rates as the decision threshold varies under a specified task and dataset.
cards.extra: An aggregate ROC can conceal subgroup-specific curves and different operational prevalence.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why does application context matter for biometric data?
cards.back: A face is difficult to change, can reveal or be linked to identity and sensitive inferences, and may be captured without meaningful consent or awareness.
cards.extra: Security, privacy, dignity, and surveillance risks differ sharply between voluntary device unlock and public-space identification.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is open-set versus closed-set recognition?
cards.back: Closed-set evaluation assumes the correct identity is in the enrolled gallery; open-set recognition allows the person to be unknown, adding a rejection or non-match decision.
cards.extra: Closed-set accuracy can overstate performance in a deployment where unknown people are common.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can benchmark results fail to predict real-world face-recognition performance?
cards.back: Deployment may differ in lighting, pose, camera quality, age, population, compression, motion, gallery size, prevalence, and operator behavior.
cards.extra: Validate the actual use conditions and report subgroup and environment slices.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does NIST FRVT demographic reporting help an analyst examine?
cards.back: Variation in face-recognition error rates across demographic groups and the role of algorithm, data, and application conditions.
cards.extra: It supplies measurement evidence, not a decision that any particular deployment is lawful or acceptable.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why is human review not an automatic fix for a biased face-recognition system?
cards.back: Reviewers can overtrust automation, lack time or information, reproduce social bias, or treat an algorithmic match as probable cause; review must have authority, training, evidence, and appeal.
cards.extra: Human-in-the-loop can distribute accountability without actually improving it.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What question should an organization ask before deploying face recognition in a public setting?
cards.back: Is the purpose necessary and proportionate, is consent or legal authority adequate, are less intrusive alternatives available, are error costs and redress acceptable, and can the organization demonstrate accountability?
cards.extra: The responsible answer may be to narrow the use, add safeguards, or not deploy.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What does a demographic differential in face-recognition performance mean?
cards.back: Error rates or other performance measures differ across demographic groups under a specified task, dataset, algorithm, threshold, and operating condition.
cards.extra: The differential is a measurement finding; interpreting its justice and policy significance requires context.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can false-positive disparities be especially harmful in surveillance?
cards.back: A false match can place an innocent person into an investigation or enforcement pipeline, and the burden may fall unevenly on groups already subject to greater surveillance.
cards.extra: Error type, base rate, institutional action, and redress determine the harm.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why should face-recognition audits report subgroup distributions, not only subgroup accuracy?
cards.back: A group can have a small sample, different image quality, different gallery prevalence, or different operational conditions that affect both estimates and harm.
cards.extra: Report denominators, uncertainty, task definition, and image or demographic coverage.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How can labels create bias in facial datasets?
cards.back: Labels may misclassify identity, gender, race, age, emotion, or other attributes; some labels are subjective or socially constructed, and errors may be concentrated in groups.
cards.extra: A model cannot be validated against a ground truth that is undefined or inconsistently assigned.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is intersectional error analysis?
cards.back: Testing combinations of attributes and conditions—such as skin tone and gender presentation or age and disability—to find failures hidden by single-attribute averages.
cards.extra: Choose slices that correspond to plausible use and harm, while handling privacy and small-cell uncertainty.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can changing a recognition threshold fail to eliminate bias?
cards.back: A single threshold may trade errors unevenly when score distributions differ by group; separate thresholds raise governance and fairness questions and can still leave data or context bias.
cards.extra: Thresholds redistribute error; they do not repair the representation or the use.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the difference between a dataset problem and a deployment problem?
cards.back: A dataset problem concerns coverage, labels, quality, or sampling in the evidence used to build or test the system; a deployment problem concerns purpose, population, environment, operator behavior, and institutional action.
cards.extra: A strong benchmark cannot authorize a harmful deployment.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why can a face-recognition accuracy improvement still be ethically unacceptable?
cards.back: The improvement may expand surveillance, remove anonymity, increase chilling effects, use nonconsensual data, or improve an application whose purpose and remedies are unjust.
cards.extra: Technical performance answers “how well under a task,” not “whether the task should exist.”
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What should a biometric impact assessment include?
cards.back: Purpose and necessity, affected communities, legal authority, data provenance and retention, subgroup performance, error pathways, security, human review, alternatives, notice, access, appeal, and sunset criteria.
cards.extra: Make a stop decision possible before deployment.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why is “the algorithm is unbiased” an incomplete claim?
cards.back: Bias can arise from data, labels, thresholds, interfaces, operators, organizational incentives, and social context even if a narrow test shows balanced model errors.
cards.extra: Audit the complete sociotechnical system and the consequences of action.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is supervised learning?
cards.back: Learning a function from examples paired with target labels or outcomes so the system can predict labels or values for new examples.
cards.extra: The labels and examples reflect a data-generating process; supervision does not guarantee that the target is desirable.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the difference between a feature and a label?
cards.back: A feature is an input supplied to the model; a label is the target the model is trained to predict or estimate.
cards.extra: A feature can be a proxy for a protected attribute even when that attribute is excluded.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: How do classification and regression differ?
cards.back: Classification predicts a category or class; regression predicts a numeric quantity, though both can produce uncertain estimates used in later decisions.
cards.extra: The choice affects loss functions, evaluation metrics, and what errors mean.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is the purpose of a validation set?
cards.back: It supports model selection, hyperparameter tuning, threshold choice, or feature decisions without spending the final test set.
cards.extra: If the validation set is repeatedly optimized until it becomes a target, its evidence becomes optimistic.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is regularization?
cards.back: A modeling strategy that penalizes complexity or constrains parameters to reduce variance and improve generalization under assumptions about the task.
cards.extra: Regularization can change subgroup performance; inspect fairness rather than assuming generalization is uniform.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why is overfitting a social-risk issue as well as a technical issue?
cards.back: A model that fails on underrepresented or shifted cases can allocate opportunities or impose scrutiny unevenly, and aggregate test performance can hide those failures.
cards.extra: Generalization must be evaluated on meaningful slices and deployment conditions.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is target leakage in a predictive model?
cards.back: A feature contains information about the outcome that would not be available at the time of the decision or is produced by the outcome itself.
cards.extra: Leakage can create a persuasive but unusable model and can interact with group-specific timing or access.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: Why is a proxy variable important even when protected attributes are removed?
cards.back: It can carry information about group membership and reproduce differential treatment while making the audit less transparent.
cards.extra: Feature removal is not the same as fairness; compare behavior and causal pathways.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is distribution shift?
cards.back: A change between training, validation, or deployment distributions, including changes in populations, environments, behavior, measurement, or label relationships.
cards.extra: Shift can alter both accuracy and fairness after launch.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What should a model card state about a predictive model?
cards.back: Intended use, out-of-scope use, training context, evaluation data, performance by relevant groups and conditions, limitations, ethical considerations, and maintenance or monitoring needs.
cards.extra: Model cards make claims conditional and inspectable.
cards.typeRationale: The prompt isolates one retrievable concept and the answer supplies its context and assumptions.

cards.front: What is a confusion matrix?
cards.back: A table of true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives for a classifier under a specified threshold and population.
